title: Short Stuff: The Retirement Curse
summary: Short Stuff episode on the "retirement curse," the idea that health and mental health decline after retirement. Josh and Chuck cite a figure of a 6% to 9% decline in mental health, a 5% to 6% increase in illness, and a 5% to 16% increase in difficulties with daily activities within five to six years of retirement for the average American, and say retirement itself is less the cause than the life changes it brings. They discuss labor statistics on Americans 65 and older still working (about 19% in 2024, down to a low of 10% in 1985), financial and health-insurance reasons to keep working, end-of-life costs, and the Harvard Study of Adult Development, where social connections emerge as the key factor for healthy aging. Advice covers strength and resistance training, balance, walking, routine, sleep and nutrition, avoiding daytime TV and isolation, learning new skills, senior centers, and volunteering or working part time.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the retirement curse
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of the retirement curse, the idea that people who are doing fine can face physical or mental health problems after retiring.

segments.title: Retirement decline statistics and why it happens
segments.summary: Josh says the retirement curse is quantifiable: within five to six years of retirement the average American shows a 6% to 9% decline in mental health, a 5% to 6% increase in illness, and a 5% to 16% increase in difficulty with daily activities. He says the cause is the life changes retirement brings, and Chuck describes losing daily structure, mental engagement, physical activity and office social contact.

segments.title: Loss of social circles after retirement
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how retirement cuts off interaction with coworkers, even for remote workers, and how many Americans lack a strong friend network outside work. Josh says this loss of social connection is probably the biggest driver of decline.

segments.title: Bureau of Labor Statistics data on older workers
segments.summary: Chuck reports Bureau of Labor Statistics figures: in 1948, 27% of people 65 and older were working, falling to a low of about 10% in 1985, then rising; in 2024 about 19% were still working, and 38% of those part-time. Josh links the 1985 low to the decline of unions and pensions, which were replaced by 401k plans.

segments.title: Financial and health insurance reasons to keep working
segments.summary: Josh says many Americans keep working because they fear outliving their savings and because employer health insurance is hard to replace, since the US lacks universal single-payer care. Chuck adds that end-of-life care is very expensive.

segments.title: Personal choice and remote work as reasons to keep working
segments.summary: Chuck says people are healthier and living longer, so many want to keep working for purpose and something to do, and remote work makes continuing easier. Josh mentions a Harvard study of 724 men followed for over 75 years.

segments.title: Harvard Study of Adult Development and social connections
segments.summary: Josh describes the Harvard study that has followed 724 men for over 75 years, with about 60 still living, and says social connections are the strongest factor for happiness, longer life and less disease. Chuck names director Robert Waldinger and his TED talk on what makes a good life.

segments.title: Physical exercise: strength training, balance and walking
segments.summary: The hosts recommend strength and resistance training alongside cardio. Josh says it keeps bones and muscles healthy, prevents sarcopenia and stooping, and improves balance to reduce falls. He also recommends regular walking outdoors.

segments.title: Daily routine, avoiding daytime TV and staying engaged
segments.summary: Chuck says a daily routine matters for mental health, along with nutrient-dense food and good sleep. Both hosts warn against sitting in front of daytime TV, especially cable news. They suggest learning new skills such as dance, instruments, or languages, and support for senior centers.
topics: learning new skills later in life

segments.title: Volunteering, mentoring and staying active in retirement
segments.summary: Josh suggests volunteering and mentoring, and both hosts say the key is to keep doing things and avoid sitting on the couch. Chuck says the retirement curse is largely self-inflicted and says he wants to be active in old age, with breakdancing as a joke.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the short stuff segment with a joke about becoming old men.

segments.title: Production credit
segments.summary: Chuck gives the iHeartRadio production credit and directs listeners to find more podcasts in the iHeartRadio app.
